entries.title: Heavy rain, flash flooding possible in Chicago area overnight
entries.summary: <p>Heavy rain and thunderstorms could bring flash flooding to the Chicago area overnight Sunday, with forecasters most concerned about the period from about 10 or 11 p.m. through early Monday.</p><p>A flood watch issued Sunday afternoon remains in effect until 7 a.m. Monday, according to the National Weather Service.</p><p>Showers and thunderstorms were developing across northwest Illinois and moving into the area Sunday evening, said Mike Bardou, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.</p><p>The storms could bring multiple rounds of heavy rainfall to some areas, Bardou said. It remained unclear Sunday evening which areas would receive the most rain.</p><p>The heaviest rainfall in the Chicago area could begin between about 10 p.m. and midnight and continue for several hours overnight, Bardou said.</p><p>“Flash flooding is one of our biggest concerns here because the rain could fall very quickly, in the order of 1 to 2 inches per hour under some of these storms, or even perhaps briefly heavier than that,” Bardou said.</p><p>Some parts of the Chicago area, including many suburbs, had already received 1 to 3 inches of rain earlier Sunday, leaving some areas saturated and potentially with standing water, Bardou said.</p><p>The weather could also affect the Monday morning commute. Bardou said the bulk of the rainfall would probably occur before daybreak, but ponding or flooding could persist into the morning, depending on how much rain falls and where.</p><p>Bardou pointed to viaducts in the city, typical high-water areas and some expressways as places where flooding or ponding could potentially linger. Damaging winds are also a concern. </p><p>The weather service issued a severe thunderstorm watch at 8:44 p.m. Sunday for Cook, DuPage and several other Illinois counties. The watch remains in effect until 4 a.m. Monday.</p><p>Bardou said damaging straight-line winds and large hail were also concerns.</p><p>“The biggest thing is it’s a good evening and overnight to stay weather aware and have a way to get woken up by warnings if you’re going to be asleep,” Bardou said.</p><p>He also urged people who live near creeks that rise quickly or in areas prone to basement flooding to monitor conditions and have a way to receive warning notifications.</p><p>As of 9:40 p.m. Sunday, ComEd reported 288 active outages affecting more than 7,900 customers.</p>

entries.title: Man fatally shot in head in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally struck in the head by gunfire in Englewood Sunday afternoon and taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, Chicago police said.</p><p>The victim was pronounced at the hospital, police said.</p><p>The victim had in the 1300 block of West 73rd Place in the Englewood neighborhood at about 4:19 p.m. when he was struck in the head by gunfire, police said.</p><p>The victim’s age remained unknown Sunday evening.</p><p>Police said there were no updates available, and the shooting remained under investigation by area detectives.</p>

entries.title: Hagen Smith earns first major-league victory in first appearance for White Sox
entries.summary: <p>Left-hander Hagen Smith earned his first major-league victory in his first major-league appearance in the oddest of ways.</p><p>The Guardians and White Sox played the first inning of their series finale Sunday at Rate Field before the heavens unexpectedly opened. Major League Baseball and the Sox saw forecasts that called for clear skies, despite heavy rain to the north. After another rough first inning for right-hander Davis Martin, his day was done.</p><p>With four lefties and four switch hitters in the Guardians’ lineup, Sox manager Will Venable chose Smith to take the ball after the rain delay, which lasted 2 hours and 23 minutes.</p><p>“I didn’t know I was going in till about an hour into the delay,” Smith said. “I was like, ‘Sounds good to me.’ ”</p><p>And it looked good to the Sox. Smith struck out the side in the second inning before walking the bases loaded in the third and escaping. When the Sox scored four runs in their third, on the strength of Colson Montgomery’s three-run homer, Smith was in line for the win.</p><p>He got it when the Sox held on for a 5-3 victory, taking the series and extending their lead in the American League Central to a season-high 3 ½ games, only now it’s over the Tigers, who are a half-game ahead of the Twins and Guardians. The Sox visit the Tigers next weekend.</p><p>The victory also gave the Sox 61 wins, one more than they had all of last season.</p><p>“It’s great. It signals progress for us,” manager Will Venable said. “Obviously, we have a long way to go here, but certainly happy about where we’re at now, knowing that we’ve gone through some stuff and continue to push through and just get better and better.”</p><p>The Sox called up Smith, along with right-hander Tanner McDougal, on Saturday. Smith, the Sox’ No. 2 prospect and 51st-ranked prospect overall, according to MLB.com, struck out 87 hitters in 58 ⅓ innings at Triple-A Charlotte this season, allowing only a .189 batting average. But he also walked 40. On Sunday, he struck out three and walked four.</p><p>“He’s got such good stuff,” Venable said. “If he’s in the zone, he’s going to be really hard to deal with. We saw that, and you understand with that stuff, it’s hard to control the movement, that there are going to be some walks in there. But as he continues to grow, you expect him to be able to tighten it up.”</p><p>“The first inning obviously was good, and then the second inning fell off a little bit,” Smith said. “You just want to go out there and compete, and the results are what they are. And it turned out to be good.”</p><p>The Sox drafted Smith fifth overall out of Arkansas in 2024. He rose through the organization each season before getting the call.</p><p>“You always dream of this growing up, especially when you get drafted,” he said. “You just look forward to the debut. It was a really special moment.”</p><p>“You have these plans to get these young guys a nice soft landing spot,” Venable said, “and the second inning after a rain delay is not something he’s done before. And then as his outing unfolded, he was challenged in his second inning with the bases loaded. It was a really good test for him and obviously came through.”</p><p>McDougal almost had his special moment, too. With righty Trevor Richards, the Sox’ seventh pitcher of the game, struggling in the ninth, Venable had McDougal warming up. Richards walked No. 9 hitter Angel Genao to start the inning, then walked Chase DeLauter one out later, bringing up Jose Ramirez as the tying run.</p><p>Ramirez hit a sacrifice fly, and Rhys Hoskins flew out to end it, giving Richards his first save of the season and third of his career — and Smith his first victory.</p><p>“I didn’t know that until I got back in the clubhouse,” Smith entries.title: Bally’s to stop work on some amenities at permanent Chicago casino development amid video gambling dispute
entries.summary: <p>Bally’s is “resetting the pace of construction” on parts of its permanent Chicago casino development in River West, the company said Sunday.</p><p>The announcement comes amid an ongoing dispute over the potential expansion of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/29/ballys-casino-river-west-lori-lightfoot-lawsuit-challenge-video-gambling-terminals" target="_blank" ><u>video gambling terminals</u></a> in the city.</p><p>Bally’s notified the Chicago Community Builders Collective on Saturday that work would stop on some of the surrounding amenities, including the hotel, event center and some restaurants.</p><p>Subcontractors were informed Sunday morning, a spokesperson said, and the work stoppage would most likely take effect Monday.</p><p>The opening of the permanent casino remains set for early 2027, the company said.</p><p>Bally’s said the city had also been alerted to the announcement.</p><p>The company said in a statement that the potential for an “uncontrolled proliferation” of video gambling terminals breaches the city’s commitment not to expand gaming under its host community agreement with Bally’s and “creates uncertainty” that could hurt the casino’s prospects.</p><p>The $16.6 billion 2026 city budget lifted Chicago’s ban on video gambling terminals. Bally’s has opposed their legalization in the city, arguing it violates the host agreement.</p><p>The $1.7 billion casino project has encountered financial and logistical challenges since Bally’s was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/5/25/23141244/ballys-casino-approved-chicago-city-council-river-west-medinah-temple-lightfoot-police-fire-pensions" target="_blank" ><u>selected</u></a> to build Chicago’s casino in 2022, including an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2024/03/12/ballys-chicago-casino-buyout-soo-kim" target="_blank" ><u>$800 million</u></a> “funding gap,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/1/22/24047289/ballys-casino-hotel-tower-plans-changes-city-hall-chicago-river" target="_blank" ><u>changes to its hotel plans</u></a> and delays that pushed the permanent casino’s expected opening into 2027.</p><p>Bally’s said Sunday the company intends to fully honor its commitments under the host agreement.</p><p>The company acknowledged the construction changes would affect many of the 1,500 union workers affiliated with the project but did not specify exactly how many would be impacted.</p><p>“We do not take this lightly because of the potential impact on many of the 1,500 union tradespeople who have been working hard to build Bally’s Chicago,” Bally’s said.</p><p>The company did not provide a timeline for when work on the affected portions of the development could resume.</p><p>Bally’s said it would continue assessing its options, which the company entries.title: Decades-old mistreatment of Japanese Americans reverberates with country's current policies
entries.summary: <p>The fear over Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor led to the signing of <a class="Link" href="https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/executive-order-9066" target="_blank" >Executive Order 9066</a> on Feb. 19, 1942, permitting the forced removal of all people of Japanese descent from their West Coast homes and into assembly centers and concentration camps. The 10 concentration camps that were constructed imprisoned 126,000 Japanese — two-thirds who were U.S. citizens.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://savingplaces.org/places/tule-lake" target="_blank" >Tule Lake</a> Segregation Center was the largest camp. It held 18,700 adults and children in a squalid overcrowded space designed to accommodate 15,000 prisoners. Just last month, the nonprofit <a class="Link" href="https://www.tulelake.org/" target="_blank" >Tule Lake Committee</a> organized its biannual four-day pilgrimage to Tule Lake, California, for descendants and survivors of this ugly chapter in American history.</p><p>Toward the end of the war, Tule Lake is where the U.S. Department of Justice set in motion an unprecedented plan that enabled the deportation of "disloyal" Japanese Americans. Public Law 78-805 was drafted on July 1, 1944, permitting U.S. citizens to renounce their citizenship. Many Japanese Americans were misled, believing if they renounced their citizenship, their families could remain together in protective custody at Tule Lake. Horribly, misinformation drove 5,461 Japanese Americans to give up their seemingly worthless birthright citizenship at Tule Lake.</p><p>Without the protection of U.S. citizenship, several thousand young men were separated from their families and interned as "enemy aliens" and deported to DOJ internment camps. The decision to give up birthright citizenship was an act done under duress, and nearly all who renounced sought restoration of their citizenship, which the Justice Department refused.</p><p>Fortunately, civil rights lawyer <a class="Link" href="http://remembrance-project.janm.org/tributes/wayne-collins.html" target="_blank" >Wayne M. Collins</a>, through his advocacy, stopped the involuntary deportations and restored citizenship to nearly all those Japanese Americans who were stripped of their birthright. But in spite of the reversal of the deportations, those who renounced their citizenship encountered decades of shame and rejection within the Japanese community.</p><p>Forty-six years after the wartime incarceration, our government <a class="Link" href="https://www.archives.gov/press/press-releases/2013/nr13-118.html" target="_blank" >recognized the error of its actions </a>with a presidential apology, redress and reparation payments to survivors.</p><p>Today's mass deportations, inhumane imprisonment conditions and attacks on birthright citizenship echo the unjust treatment experienced by Japanese Americans during World War II. When will we stop making the same grievous mistakes?</p><p><i>Michael Harada, Wilmette</i><br><i>Barbara Takei, Sacramento, California</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f20000" name="module-f20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Aiming high for state’s Department of Natural Resources</h3><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has built one of the <a class="Link" href="https://rmi.org/resources/state-climate-action-updated-scorecards-tracking-progress-to-2030/" target="_blank" >strongest climate action records in the country</a> and now has the chance to make it even stronger. Healthy, resilient nature is a key part of the equation, one that can drive more economic investment. A transformational appointment for the next director of the <a class="Link" href="https://dnr.illinois.gov/" target="_blank" >Illinois Department of Natural Resources</a> can extend his leadership through visionary investment in nature.</p><p>The department's mission is to steward the state’s natural resources for the health of ecosystems and the well-being of residents. That extends beyond state parks to ensuring that all of Illinois’ lands and waters are healthy and beautiful.</p><p>People choose where to live based on quality of life. Access to parks, trails, clean water and vibrant natural areas is exactly what makes a place feel compelling. It's why families put down roots and why young professionals choose one city over another. Businesses know this, too. When they're deciding where to locate and how to attract talent, they look for places their employees want to live.</p><p>As a former chair of the Forest Preserves of Cook County’s Conservation and Policy Council, I saw firsthand how good leadership can nurture the land and local communities. Deer Grove East Forest Preserve is one such success story. An <a class="Link" href="https://openlands.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/rpt_dge_econ_valuation_final_10102016.pdf" target="_blank" >economic analysis of the restoration work</a> found that every dollar spent on restoration delivered an immediate $2 return from jobs and economic activity. In the long term, it delivered a whopping $6 return from flood control, water quality benefits and recreational activity. At the scale of the state, the health and economic benefits of this type of conservation are indisputable.</p><p>Cook County voters understand this and responded in 2022 by passing, with an <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2023/10/17/cook-county-forest-preserves-189-million-budget-marks-new-era-with-referendum-cash/" target="_blank" >overwhelming majority, a ballot measure</a> that increases investment in nature by $45 million a year. The five collar counties followed suit in 2024, generating over $1 billion over the next 20 years for nature.</p><p>There’s real headroom here. Illinois has lost more than 99% of the state’s original prairie and over 85% of its historic wetlands, and ranks 49th in the nation in protected natural areas per capita — a clear marker of fragmented habitats. As climate change reshapes ecosystems across the country, Illinois has the chance to step up and lead.</p><p>We love the Prairie State. The governor loves it, too. A transformational appointment for the Illinois Department of Natural Resources is his opportunity to write the next chapter of that legacy.</p><p><i>Wendy J. Paulson, executive chairwoman, Bobolink Foundation</i></p><h3>Trump doesn’t deserve to be called a leader</h3><h3></h3><p>I take issue with David McGrath's recent op-ed headlined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/07/31/president-donald-trump-cold-blooded-leader-death-iran-ice-shootings-covid-measles-david-mcgrath" target="_blank" >“Trump is our cold-blooded leader.”</a> I do not take issue with the atrocities and unlawfulness McGrath noted about the Trump administration. However, I disagree with his describing Trump as a "leader."</p><p>According to Merriam-Webster, leadership means "the office or position of a leader," "a capacity to lead" and "the act or instance of leading." I fail to see any "leadership" qualities — as well as integrity, honesty, accountability, responsibility, empathy, compassion — in Trump as he's pushed the country to the economic brink with his tariffs, endangered us in an unwinnable war in the Middle East and dismissed higher education and science as the bases of government.</p><p>Words have meaning, as McGrath surely knows. I think we need to be careful in calling Trump a "leader." I describe him as the "occupier" of the White House, but I'll leave it up to Professor McGrath to find a more appropriate moniker or epithet.</p><p><i>Linda Hendelman, West Ridge</i></p>

entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have friends who are kind, intelligent and warm. However, as we have spent more time with them, "Phyllis'" compulsive talking has become a real problem for us. She hijacks whichever one of us is sitting next to her and starts a monologue that goes on and on.</p><p>Phyllis doesn't even look at the person she's talking to and doesn't hear when you try to interject anything. She has said she's hard of hearing and does wear a hearing aid, but I believe the problem is more than a hearing deficit.</p><p>The dilemma is they have booked a cruise with us. We didn't ask them to, but when I mentioned we were going, they thought it would be fun. The thought of having dinner together every night and being subjected to this is going to put a distinct damper on what is a rare vacation for my husband and me. Is there any way to not offend them and have more give-and-take in the conversation? — <i>DREADING IT IN OREGON</i></p><p><b>DEAR DREADING IT:</b> You or your husband need to make clear to this couple well before the ship sets sail that you signed up for this cruise because you want to spend time alone together, meet new people and make new friends, which is why you will not be able to dine with them every night or participate in every activity with them. Period.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My wife of 48 years recently died, and my stepson put some artificial flowers on her grave. I was surprised to see this when I visited on the eight-month anniversary of her death. Both my wife and I always considered artificial flowers tacky and not appropriate for cemeteries, even though lots of people decorate gravesites with them.</p><p>I haven't said anything to him about my feelings about plastic flowers, but I would like to prevent more of them from being placed when these fade away. How can I ask him to not put any more plastic flowers on the grave, or should I just ignore it? I'm less likely to visit her grave when these flowers are there. — <i>MOURNING IN ALABAMA</i></p><p><b>DEAR MOURNING:</b> Your stepson may not realize how his mother felt about plastic flowers, so mention it to him the next time you talk. If he doesn't visit his mother's grave often, he may not realize that they have been removed, which I suggest you do if seeing them would discourage your visits.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've been married for 40 years, but it's a platonic relationship with no communication on his part. I must run the household, make sure bills get paid and be responsible for everything — whatever life throws at us. My health is waning, and I'm concerned for my future. I have tried talking, counseling, etc., to no avail. What do I do? — <i>FED UP IN UTAH</i></p><p><b>DEAR FED UP:</b> Because, after 40 years, you are finally fed up enough that you might actually do something about it, I'm suggesting some sessions with a different counselor than the one you have been seeing. You stated that you are the one who takes care of the house, pays the bills, etc. Has your husband been earning the money? If so, then you might also benefit from interviewing several attorneys about what your options might be if you no longer wish to carry the whole load alone.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: CPS budget challenges Springfield to pay up
entries.summary: <p>Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you know the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" >$9.96 billion budget Chicago Public Schools passed</a> for the coming fiscal year is generating some controversy. OK, so whenever CPS does anything it engenders controversy. But in this case, some legitimate issues are on the table.</p><p>That’s because in a split vote, the CPS Board passed a budget that includes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/04/mayor-brandon-johnson-cps-budget-schools-funding-tif-surplus-springfield-state-funding" >$150 million in state funding</a> the Illinois<b> </b>General Assembly hasn’t authorized. The board members who voted for the budget noted the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/07/31/emanuel-chris-welch-chicago-teachers-union-public-schools-cps-ctu-rich-miller" >speaker of the House</a> and Senate president have publicly indicated a willingness to get more state funding for CPS this year, and including the extra $150 million averted the need to lay off roughly <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2026/07/30/cps-board-members-pass-last-minute-amended-budget-assuming-150m-more-state-revenue" target="_blank" >760 teachers, 800 or so support personnel and 41 assistant principals</a>.</p><p>Those who opposed the budget aver it’s not fiscally prudent to bake dollars into CPS spending that haven’t been appropriated by state lawmakers and could hurt the CPS credit rating. While acknowledging key state legislative leaders have voiced support for bumping Illinois investment in CPS, the board members who voted no emphasize those legislative leaders haven’t identified any specific dollar amount of additional funding. They’re also concerned the political pathway to getting more money for CPS is difficult, especially during the veto session, when a supermajority vote is required to pass legislation.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-860000" name="module-860000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>The imbroglio over the CPS budget is heated. But if everyone takes a deep breath, it also affords a rare opportunity to consider fiscal concerns in context of the larger public policy issues being implicated — in this case, education funding.</p><p>In 2017, Illinois replaced its former school funding formula, which was then derided as the least-equitable in the country, with the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2024/08/02/illinois-fully-funding-public-schools-evidence-based-formula-education" > Evidence-Based Funding for Student Success Act</a> or EBF. The EBF ties school funding to covering the cost of those educational practices that research shows actually enhance student achievement, on everything from test scores, to graduation rates and college matriculation rates. Tying taxpayer dollars to paying for what’s been proven to work academically is really good public policy.</p><p>When it passed, the funding formula called for the state to fully fund it within 10 years, which would be this year. But that hasn’t happened. In fact, the aggregate shortfall in K-12 funding has increased each of the last three years and currently sits at $4.2 billion. That means most Illinois school districts — including CPS — still don’t have the resources needed to fund those educational practices the research shows work.</p><p>So why’s that problematic? Well, over the last few decades, the economic importance of educational attainment has grown significantly. All the data shows that individuals with college degrees have lower rates of unemployment and higher incomes than those who don’t complete college. </p><h3>Shortchanging students</h3><p>Consider that in 1979, the median earnings of full-time workers with a bachelor’s degree <a class="Link" href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/bernanke20070206a.htm" target="_blank" >were 38% greater</a> on average than workers with just a high school diploma. By 2024, that wage gap had jumped to 84%. Moreover, communities with a greater number of college-educated folks have lower crime rates, better overall health and higher wages for all workers, not just those with postsecondary degrees. The Federal Reserve of Cleveland even found that states with the best high school and college graduation rates also have the highest per capita personal incomes.</p><p>And this trend isn’t going away. The Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce found by 2031, <a class="Link" href="https://cew.georgetown.edu/cew-reports/projections2031/" target="_blank" >72% of jobs</a> will require some postsecondary education credential. Which in turn means the K-12 education students receive has to be of sufficient quality for them to develop the numeracy and literacy skills needed to graduate and gain that post-high school credential. Hence, shortchanging public schools equates to shortchanging the ability of the students who attend them to make it in the modern economy.</p><p>So who are the students being shortchanged? In the case of CPS, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2024/05/14/cps-chicagoans-school-grade-students-not-learning-enough-survey" >71% are low-income</a>, 80% are Black or Brown, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/about/stats-facts/" target="_blank" >27%</a> are English learners. The vast majority of these children have been denied opportunity throughout their young lives. Getting a quality K-12 education, however, will arm them with the academic skills needed to pursue higher education and become qualified for the type of jobs that’ll make them economically self-sufficient.</p><p>Unfortunately, last year CPS <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/07/23/chicago-public-schools-budget-deficit" >had $985 million</a> less than what the evidence indicated it needed to provide an adequate education to its students. So those board members who approved the new CPS budget decided to put some pressure on state lawmakers to close $150 million of that gap this year.</p><p>And if the additional state funding doesn’t materialize? CPS could offset the shortage by implementing the roughly $145 million in cuts from furlough days and midyear hiring freezes it previously identified but put off implementing until it sees whether the General Assembly steps up to the plate. That seems, well reasonable, even if not ideal from a pure budgetary policy standpoint.</p><p><i>Ralph Martire is executive director of the Center for Tax and Budget Accountability, a nonpartisan fiscal policy think tank, and the Arthur Rubloff Professor of Public Policy at Roosevelt University.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-130000" name="module-130000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Firms linked to 2 men convicted of corruption have gotten campaign business from JB Pritzker and the CTU
entries.summary: <p>Two political campaign firms with close ties to men with public corruption convictions have gotten business in recent years in Chicago and statewide political races, including the current, hotly contested race for Chicago School Board president and more than $1.5 million from Gov. JB Pritzker in his gubernatorial campaigns, records show.</p><p>In the governor’s campaigns, about $1.2 million went to a firm formed by a former Illinois Department of Children and Family Services deputy director, Bamani Obadele, who pleaded guilty in 2010 to a state contracting scheme under former Gov. Rod Blagojevich. Obadele was sentenced to six months in jail and ordered to repay more than $80,000.</p><p>Pritzker’s gubernatorial campaigns also spent more than $420,000 with the firm tied to Isaac “Ike” Carothers, a former Chicago City Council member who pleaded guilty in 2010 to taking $40,000 in home improvements from a developer who wanted to build homes in an industrial area in Carothers’ 29th Ward on the West Side.</p><p>In the school board race, the Chicago Teachers Union has spent more than $36,000 with the two firms and a company tied to a campaign worker, Karina Escobar-Perez, who pleaded guilty last year to forging signatures on campaign petitions in Indiana for the presidential race. The CTU work was for the campaign of Hilario Dominguez, whom the teachers union endorsed in June for school board president in a five-way race.</p><p>Dominguez’ campaign has reported $99,500 in contributions as of its latest filings, on Aug. 5. All of that was in-kind contributions from the CTU, and about one-third was to firms linked to Obadele, Carothers and Escobar-Perez.</p><p>The CTU’s political organization has used Carothers’ and Obadele’s firms in other school board races, and all three companies have done extensive work in other political races.</p><p>The Dominguez campaign did not respond to questions about the firms.</p><p>The governor’s campaign did not answer questions about Obadele’s and Carothers’ work but said: “The campaign hires consultants who are experienced and well-known organizers in their communities.”</p><p>A CTU spokeswoman said the people and groups they contracted with as “vendors are the same as those hired by Gov. Pritzker, Rep. [Margaret] Croke, and numerous other candidates.” In her statement, she didn't explain those choices, focusing instead on their endorsed candidates: "What voters should know about the candidates we are supporting is that they will be the fiercest advocates for Chicago's children instead of administrators of unnecessary cuts to their education.”</p><p>Pritzker is seeking reelection this year, again running against Republican Darren Bailey, whom he defeated by more than 12 percentage points in 2022. In 2018, Pritzker defeated incumbent Gov. Bruce Rauner by more than 15 percentage points.</p><p>Pritzker, who was among contenders to be Kamala Harris’ 2024 vice presidential running mate, has been attending political events across the entries.title: One down, one to go: Exterior construction wraps up at the first of two towers at 400 N. Lake Shore
entries.summary: <p>After more than two years of construction, Chicagoans can now see what the residential tower built on the spot of the proposed Chicago Spire will look like — from the outside, at least — once completed.</p><p>Exterior construction wrapped up late last month on the 72-story skyscraper at 400 N. Lake Shore Drive, with the installation of the building's last piece of facade glass.</p><p>That means what we now see of the 857-foot tall glass building is what we'll get. Exterior work on the north tower is complete.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by Related Midwest</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>What do I think of the building?</p><p>I'm holding off until it's completed sometime in 2027. But I will say, the building has an overall power and elegance that could be diminished if the second tower isn't built.</p><p>And I have to say this, though: SOM claims the waterfall-like windows are a modern interpretation of the classic Chicago bay window. But as a person who grew up in a house with a two-story bay window, I struggle to see the visual connection.</p><p>That's not a knock against 400 N. Lake Shore's windows. They are among the building's better features.</p><p>And it's no Chicago Spire — nor does it have to be, said Chicago Architecture Center CEO Eleanor Gorski, an architect and former high-ranking city planning official.</p><p>"You see [buildings like this] being pursued all in the Middle East and Far East," she said. "But I almost feel like Chicago has outgrown having to do that. I think that we take advantage of whatever scale we have and look for the best architectural outcomes."</p><p>Gorski added, "Frankly from an urban design standpoint, I think it maybe it would have been a little gruesome to have this gigantic tower there."</p>

entries.title: National pediatrics group says all kids 6 months and older should receive flu shot
entries.summary: <p>The American Academy of Pediatrics is urging children ages 6 months and older receive this year's flu shot. The Illinois-based organization is making the recommendation before any federal agencies release their own guidelines for the upcoming flu season.</p><p>Last year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention removed its long-time universal recommendation for the annual flu shot from its childhood vaccine schedule. Instead, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/05/us-drops-the-number-of-vaccines-it-recommends-for-every-child" target="_blank" >the CDC only said</a> certain "high-risk" groups need to get the shot or when doctors recommend it in what’s called “shared decision-making.”</p><p>In the organization's statement, the pediatric organization emphasized the safety and benefits of the shot, especially after nearly 200 children died from the flu during the 2025-2026 flu season. Yet less than 50% of children ages 6 months to 17 years were vaccinated, according to the the group.</p><p>“The good news is flu vaccines have been thoroughly studied,” said Dr. Kristina Bryant, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics' Committee on Infectious Diseases.</p><p>“We know they are safe in children and they can prevent not just hospitalizations and death but every year they prevent a substantial number of illnesses that result in trips to the doctor’s office," Bryant said in a statement. "We want to keep kids healthy and going to school and parents healthy and going to work. Flu vaccines can help us accomplish that.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-abstract/158/2/e2026076453/208191/Influenza-Vaccine-Effectiveness-Against-Pediatric?redirectedFrom=fulltext" target="_blank" >A recent CDC study</a> found the flu shot reduces the risk of kids and teens dying from the virus by 80%. During the 2024-2025 flu season, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu-burden/php/data-vis-vac/index.html" target="_blank" >the CDC estimates</a> the vaccine prevented nearly 15,000 hospitalizations and 245 deaths in children and teens.</p><p>The American Academy of Pediatrics noted the CDC has yet to release new flu vaccine recommendations.</p><p>The pediatrics group recommends that children receive the vaccine as soon as it becomes available — ideally by the end of October, ahead of flu season. Pregnant and breastfeeding people are also encouraged to get the shot to protect themselves and their infants.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/09/10/covid-19-vaccines-arrive-at-chicago-pharmacies-as-pediatricians-wait-for-doses-and-guidance" target="_blank" >Pediatricians have previously told the Sun-Times</a> it's best for everyone to get their flu shot just before winter because the vaccine works best in the eight to 12 weeks after getting it.</p>
